analysis.one_liner: Reinstates taxes on polluting industries to fund the cleanup of toxic waste sites.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate Superfund polluter taxes was referred to committee, never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Until 1995, a tax on petroleum and chemical companies paid for it; when that tax lapsed, cleanup costs shifted to regular taxpayers. This bill would have brought those taxes back, charging oil, chemical, and other corporations roughly the same rates as before to refill the cleanup fund through 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream from contaminated sites, and taxpayers generally, because cleanup funding would come from the industries that created the pollution instead of the Treasury. The Environmental Protection Agency's Superfund trust fund would regain a dedicated revenue stream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, a per-barrel tax on crude oil and petroleum products, through the end of 2015.
Reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, a supplemental corporate income tax originally imposed on large chemical and petroleum companies, for taxable years through 2015.
Removes a loophole so the excise tax applies to imported petroleum rather than only domestic production, by striking the export-related exemptions in the tax code.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, petroleum importers, and large chemical and petrochemical companies, which would pay the reinstated excise tax and corporate environmental income tax. Those costs could partly reach consumers through prices, and a share of the excise tax falls on petroleum products generally.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax applies to petroleum products broadly, so some of the cost would likely pass through to consumers at the pump rather than being borne only by polluters.

Restoring a corporate tax through 2016 imposes new costs on energy and chemical firms and their shareholders at a time of rising energy prices, which the bill's opponents would cite as a competitive disadvantage for U.S. industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift cleanup costs for abandoned toxic waste sites from general taxpayers back onto the industries associated with the pollution, restoring the original funding design of the Superfund program. The main tradeoff is that petroleum taxes partially reach consumers and add costs to energy and chemical producers. The tax rates are a restoration of lapsed levies, not a new invention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on October 24, 2007, to reinstate the lapsed Superfund financing taxes through the end of 2015.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation; no further action was taken.
The bill never came to the House floor and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, petroleum importing, and chemical companies are better off, since the reinstated excise tax and corporate environmental income tax never took effect, leaving Superfund cleanups funded by general taxpayer revenues instead. Communities awaiting toxic-site cleanup gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the Superfund polluter taxes through 2015.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 24, 2007 and never reported it out or scheduled any action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition cannot be measured from the record; the bill simply died in committee with a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Oil and petroleum refiners and importers
industries.note: The bill reinstates the per-barrel Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on crude oil and petroleum products, including imports, through 2015. The industry's interest in the bill's defeat ran against the public interest in having polluters rather than taxpayers fund toxic-site cleanup.

The bill reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, a supplemental corporate tax originally aimed at large chemical and petroleum firms, for years through 2015. Avoiding this tax shifts cleanup costs to general taxpayers.
A refilled Superfund trust fund means more federally funded cleanup work at hazardous waste sites, which supports firms that perform that work and benefits communities near those sites.
